title: The Spirit creates with the Father and the Son: “Let us make man”
english: …again and warmed it back to life: the Holy Spirit did, without toil and as if of his own accord, being fellow-creator and equal in working with God, the master craftsman who gave the earth its being in the beginning. So we are permitted to know from what these have declared. Job: “A divine Spirit made me, and the breath of the Almighty teaches me” (Job 33:4). David, in the hundred and fourth Psalm: “You will send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 104:30). The apostle confirms this, writing to the Corinthians the second time: “So if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). And in the thirty-third Psalm: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6).

Do not run past what can be heard straight from these words. See rather that the Spirit of God, as creator and good God, abiding for ever, supplies the creation with a lasting friendship, has bound it fast with bonds that cannot be loosed, and has set it firm. Unshaken, he also upholds all things by his own power. See too that it is unlawful to call a creature him who creates and gives strength to the creatures of God. For the psalmist, presenting him in a hidden way as God’s fellow-worker and of one essence with God, since he is his Spirit and his finger, as was shown in the first book, prophesies in the eighth Psalm: “For I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Psalm 8:3).

Moses too, in Genesis, speaking for God the Father to the Son and to his Holy Spirit, says: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness, and let them rule over the things on the earth” (Genesis 1:26). For God did not take angels or other spirits as fellow-workers or advisers, “since the servant does not know what his master is doing” (John 15:15). Nor is he ever found to have taken a creature along with him for the work of creation, as David sings in the thirty-third Psalm: “He who fashioned their hearts by himself alone” (Psalm 33:15); and in the hundred and thirty-ninth: “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret” (Psalm 139:15). And as Paul writes to the Romans: “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Romans 11:34); that is, no one in creation. For the word “who,” being broad, makes this plain.

By not saying “Make” but “Let us make,” he showed that the Son and the Holy Spirit are not underlings, but of one power and one will; and by adding “according to our image and likeness,” that the Trinity has one essence. He showed too that this was not said to angels, who have “the image and likeness” in a measure infinitely and incomparably less, if it is safe for one who is only a man to say this of the Trinity, which has no form, no shape, and is beyond speech. Therefore the same writer of the world’s making added: “And God made man; according to the image of God he made him; male and female he made them, and he blessed them” (Genesis 1:27-28); and again: “God saw that it was good.” In these words, once more, the perfection, harmony, ordering beauty and all-embracing bounty of the self-complete Trinity, author of all that comes to be, are signified in a hidden way. For Moses, or rather God who sounded these words in his ears, did not think them fit for theatres and the crowd, but only for as many as would not sin against them. For “God made” (that is, the Son) “man according to the image of God” (that is, of the Father), “he made him; and God saw” (that is, the Spirit) “that it was good, and he blessed them,” that is, he sanctified them.

“According to the image,” as it seems to me, should be understood in this way: that from the divine breathing we have the immortal spirit, and a mind ever in motion and steering toward what it ought, and wise speech, pleasing to the one who gave it, which with faith can become the cause of the begetting of children, of life, of the raising of the dead and of the moving of mountains; and besides these, that we have also received a share in his goodness.

Then Paul too, as was said a little before: “He will give life also to our mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in us” (Romans 8:11). And to the Hebrews, proclaiming that the ages came into being and the creation was made firm by the Holy Spirit, and calling the Spirit the word of God, as has already been mentioned, he writes: “By faith we understand that the ages were framed by the word of God, so that what is seen did not come into being from things that appear” (Hebrews 11:3); and again: “For he upholds all things by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3). And the psalmist: “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 104:24), that is, in your Spirit and in your Son. How, then, is the divine Spirit not without beginning, and creator, and God in the proper sense? He is inseparable from him who breathed him forth and from the creator Son; he built the ages, and with them were brought forth heaven, what is in it, and everything else that is created; he bears and governs all things by his own power; he, at the very moment of the …

added_allusions.reason: “God saw that it was good” is the refrain of Genesis 1:10-25; Didymus applies it to the making of man, which Genesis 1:31 closes with “very good”. No single verse has his exact words about man.
“From the divine breathing we have the immortal spirit” (ἐκ τοῦ θεϊκοῦ φυσήματος) recalls God breathing the breath of life into Adam.
Speech that “with faith” can move mountains recalls Matthew 17:20 (also Mark 11:23; 1 Corinthians 13:2); no words are quoted.

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: To sanctify is to create: the Spirit renews, and overshadowed the incarnation
english: …coming into being of heaven, earth and sea, was borne upon the water and made it bring forth and nourish life (Genesis 1:2)? For just as Job’s saying about the Son, “who alone stretched out the heaven” (Job 9:8), does not shut out from the work of creation the Father, from whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6) and in whom all things hold together (Colossians 1:17), for how else could these words still be true? So neither is it holy to thrust the Spirit of God, the Spirit of wisdom and power and holiness, out of being fellow-creator with God.

And what greater proof of this could be found than that the Spirit of God, day by day, in baptism renews and sanctifies, and calls us back to the better and first pattern of life? This is shown too by its being named in the same breath as creating: so the apostle, speaking of those who are expected to be made whole by the new birth and to enjoy the achievement greatest of all, cries out: “that you may become according to the image of him who created you” (Colossians 3:10); and David too prophesies in the hundred and second Psalm: “A people being created shall praise the Lord” (Psalm 102:18). If the Spirit had no fellowship of essence, of lordship and of working with the Father and with the Son, “through whom all things came to be” (John 1:3), he would not renew and sanctify.

That is why Christ, after the resurrection, re-creating and sanctifying with the all-holy Spirit the man who had been ruined by disobedience, breathed into the faces of the disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). So he fulfilled the prophecy of Nahum, which, out of an irrepressible longing for the boundless beauty of the event, tells what was still to come as if it were already being done: “He who breathes into your face has gone up from the earth, and he rescues you from affliction” (Nahum 2:1).

That to sanctify, which the divine Spirit by nature does, is also to create, David testifies when he sings: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10); that is, sanctify me, so that I may be renewed, ruined as I am by sin. For how else could another heart have been created for him? And he joins to this: “And renew a right spirit in my inmost parts” (Psalm 51:10). This stands for: grant me your venerable Spirit, who surpasses all things, so that, he says, made pure and shown so by his sanctification, I may become his worthy temple. For only through the oversight of him and of your Son do you yourself, Master, set your seal upon us; and we receive a remedy for all evils, and come to stand in sure hopes of every eternal good. It is plain to us, then, that David asks for this Spirit to be renewed in him; otherwise how could the spirit he already had be renewed as though it were only now coming upon him?

Scripture, moreover, knowing that to sanctify is greater and more needful than to create, said of pitiable Judas, who lost his sanctification: “It would have been good for that man if he had not been born” (Matthew 26:24); because, it says, he did the most ruinous thing of all: he sold his Master, who had done him no wrong, and bartered life for pieces of silver.

And indeed, concerning the form of the servant in the ineffable dispensation, of which John says, “And the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), and Paul, “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7): Solomon said, “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Proverbs 9:1), and Matthew, because the divine nature and working are the same, set it out thus: “Now the birth of Jesus Christ was in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:18). The archangel too said: “For what has been begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20); and again: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one to be born will be called Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:35).

We must remember, then, that because of the idle talk of the heretics the evangelist set the ‘coming into being’ of the incarnation first, and then the ‘birth’. For they disparage our proofs from Scripture and ask, in mock inquiry: “Is Christ, then, the son of the Spirit?” They hear with faith neither these words nor what he said to the apostles: “You do not know of what spirit the Son of Man is” (Luke 9:55).

If, then, because the Father is true God, his working is for that reason divine in every way and altogether, then, since the working of the Holy Spirit is seen to be equal and like to his, for that reason the Spirit too is true God. And it would be fitting to say the same of the Son. Otherwise, if the Father’s working were better than the Son’s or the Spirit’s, why would the Spirit or the Son work upon us at all, bringing the inferior power, if indeed they are unlike him, as the heretics say? But if the fulfilment brought by the Son and the Spirit is useful and saving, then unlike in no respect will be the …

title: The Spirit who created also renews: against the argument from craftsmen
english: …Son or the Spirit. For neither would the Most High, who is rich in mercy (Ephesians 2:4), have borrowed from one inferior and poorer, nor would we have been worked upon in two ways, and unequally. And indeed, what sense does it make that a man should be the maker and craftsman of good things, say, or of bad, while the Spirit is not? A man does this or that by God’s permission; and out of a substance that God has supplied beforehand he fashions whatever lifeless thing he may wish, but not the substance itself, as we have already said. The Spirit, however, makes with sovereign authority, and brings substance into being out of things that are not, as fellow-worker and “breath of the Almighty” (Job 33:4).

This is why God in Ezekiel, showing that our spirit is renewed while the Holy Spirit renews, and that this is not simply a spirit but properly his own, declares: “And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will give you; I will take away the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh; and my Spirit I will put in you” (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

But these men, making light even of these divine words and finding themselves at a complete loss for just arguments, have at last resorted to the arts of outsiders, and try to shift onto this thing and that what has been said so clearly. For they say, in these very words: “The dead, those who are put to death, are raised only by him who created them. A painter would not repair a master builder’s work when it decays, nor would a hunter repair a shipwright’s, nor a runner a house-builder’s; no, a master builder repairs a master builder’s work, and a shipwright a shipwright’s. But the Holy Spirit,” he says, “neither raised the dead nor created. For human nature,” he says, “was created once, in Adam; no other has been created besides it, nor has it been created many times. Even Eve was created together with Adam by the common principle of nature, and was given her own form afterwards.”

But we who are orthodox, since creating and raising the dead are above all the mark of divine power, confess that the Holy Spirit, who has done these things, is God. For “by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6). And since from the beginning, when all things were being created, he was present with God and was inseparable from him in Godhead and in working, for that reason he is also present with him and named with him when they are being renewed. For, as these very men have said, to renew belonged to no other essence, that is, nature, than that of the one who created. So it is of those who exist and live as though they did not exist, but are now being created spiritually and in a more divine way, that David and Paul preach, as was said before and as we shall find in many places. Indeed, all my time would fail me if I chose to mention every passage everywhere.

If, then, it had not seemed one thing to the Scriptures and another to these men, then first, they would at some point have taken to heart the divine writings recalled in this book and in the one before it. For what would they say, when they heard them, that the one who uttered these oracles teaches? Second, they would have reasoned that, just as the Father is co-maker by his good pleasure when the Son creates, so too is his Spirit. And they would not have dragged the things of the blessed Trinity, which mingles with nothing and which made us too, craftsmen of words and of the shaping of materials, into comparison with things unlike it: things that need one another’s help and the help of time, and do not carry out their purpose readily and blamelessly in every respect. So they say what they ought never to have said. For what could we say (and how great are we?) to God the Father, who had but once to will it, and all things came to be through the Son, the Word?

Certainly, of him who is of the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), of Abraham, and of the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:10), it has been proclaimed, as was said just now: “For what has been begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20); so that from this too it may be agreed that the sanctifying Spirit was fellow-worker with the Creator who works good. That is why it is written again: “Jesus was led in the Spirit into the wilderness” (Luke 4:1); for the guiding Spirit was with him, as God with God, and as one who holds all things together and is present everywhere, with him on whom all things are founded, who is in all things and fills all things. Otherwise, by their reasoning and their way of arguing, neither would the Father be creator or raiser of the dead. For all things came to be through the Son (John 1:3), without toil; for toil is a passion, and passion is a road to corruption.

We say these things without denying that the Master took flesh, without sin, from the nature of Adam, that is, from the Virgin, in other words from our own nature. Rather, we even confirm it by saying that from …

added_allusions.reason: “All my time would fail me” (ἐπιλείψει με ... ὁ πᾶς χρόνος) echoes “the time would fail me” in Hebrews 11:32; a turn of phrase, not a quotation.

The Spirit “who holds all things together” (πάντα συνέχων) echoes Greek Wisdom 1:7, “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which holds all things together (τὸ συνέχον τὰ πάντα)”; checked by hand, not in the KJV data.
“Who fills all things” (πληροῦντι τὰ πάντα), said of the Son, recalls Ephesians 4:10 and 1:23.
“The guiding Spirit” (τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν πνεῦμα) is the phrase of Greek Psalm 50:14 (English 51:12, 'thy free spirit'); Didymus may be recalling it.
